title: V3-6 — Reading Cracks: The Diagnostic Alphabet
summary: A crack is a message; the pattern tells you who sent it. Six authors with six signatures — plastic shrinkage, drying shrinkage, thermal, settlement, structural overload, corrosion — and the manager's rules: direction and location first, active vs dormant second, pattern over width, and in a chloride climate every crack is also a corrosion door. PLAIN: cracks are handwriting. PRO: flexural at midspan, diagonal shear at supports, delamination along the bar lines.

sections.heading: The six authors
sections.body: PLAIN & PRO, paired per author: (1) PLASTIC SHRINKAGE — first hours of a pour: shallow, parallel, mid-slab cracks like dried mud; the surface dried faster than the concrete could supply water — your sun-and-breeze climate's most common pour-day defect, cosmetic-to-minor, prevented by S2's hot-weather kit. PRO: 'plastic shrinkage from high evap rate — should've fogged and covered.' (2) DRYING SHRINKAGE — weeks to months: fine, fairly straight cracks at regular intervals or at re-entrant corners (inside corners of L-shapes are stress concentrators — why slab-opening corners get diagonal bars). PRO: 'shrinkage cracking — look at the joint layout.' (3) THERMAL — like shrinkage but tracking temperature history; big pours that got hot inside crack as the core cools. PRO: 'thermal gradient cracking; should've been treated as mass concrete.' (4) SETTLEMENT — V3-4's stair-steps through masonry, diagonals radiating from door/window corners, width taper telling you which side dropped. Structural until proven otherwise. PRO: 'differential settlement — get levels and monitor.' (5) STRUCTURAL/OVERLOAD — located exactly where V3-1 says tension lives: flexural cracks on the tension face at midspan, diagonal shear cracks near supports at ~45°. The member is talking about its capacity. Engineer, NOW. PRO: 'flexural at midspan / diagonal shear at the support — get the EOR out here.' (6) CORROSION — cracks running ALONG the rebar lines, rust staining, eventually spalls: the steel expanding inside. Your climate's long-fuse killer. PRO: 'delamination along the bar — chain-drag/covermeter survey.'

sections.heading: The manager's rules
sections.body: PLAIN: Direction and location first — cracks form perpendicular to the pull, so the crack's geometry points back at the force. Active vs dormant second — put a gauge on it and re-read: a moving crack is a live problem, a dormant one is history. Width matters less than pattern — a hairline in the WRONG place (45° at a beam support) beats a wide one in the right place (mid-panel shrinkage). And in your chloride climate, every crack is a corrosion door — sealing has value even when structure is fine. PRO: hairline <0.3 mm generally cosmetic in dry interiors but SEALABLE in marine exposure; gauges read monthly; chain-drag survey $0.05–0.15/sf; no joints = random map cracking on the slab's own schedule.

quiz.prompt: A 45° diagonal crack appears near a condo transfer-beam support. Which author, and what's the first hour's response?

choices.text: Structural — diagonal shear cracking at a support is the member talking about its capacity; the EOR is on the phone in the first hour, the area below gets shored/cordoned, and nobody 'monitors' an active shear crack casually
choices.why: Correct. Location (support) + orientation (45°) = shear signature, on the one member type (transfer beam) carrying a column's whole tributary load. This is the page-the-engineer pattern.

choices.text: Shrinkage — concrete cracks, it's what it does
choices.why: Shrinkage cracks are fine, fairly straight, mid-panel, pattern-spaced. A 45° diagonal AT A SUPPORT is the geometry of shear — the one misdiagnosis you cannot afford.

choices.text: Thermal — big transfer beams run hot curing
choices.why: Thermal cracking in mass pours is real but appears during/after curing with its own pattern. A service-stage diagonal at the support reads structural until the EOR says otherwise.

Settlement's signature is stair-steps and corner diagonals in MASONRY, tapering widths. In a concrete transfer beam, the 45° support diagonal outranks every other hypothesis — engineer first, levels later.

quiz.explanation: PLAIN: a slanted crack next to where a big beam sits on its support is the beam saying 'I'm struggling' — that call goes to the engineer within the hour. PRO: 'diagonal shear cracking at the support — shore below, cordon, EOR on site today.' (V3-6, V3-1)

quiz.teach: The two-register explanation is a skill: the same truth for a buyer and for your engineer.
quiz.prompt: An owner walkthrough finds hairline mid-panel cracks in the garage slab. What's the calm, correct, two-register handling?

choices.text: PLAIN for the buyer: 'concrete shrinks slightly as it dries and these hairlines are that — cosmetic, sealed as part of punch, and here's the gauge showing they're not moving.' PRO in the file: 'drying shrinkage, <0.3mm, dormant per gauge, sealed per marine-exposure practice' — and the closing stays on schedule
choices.why: Correct. The pattern (fine, mid-panel, straight) is shrinkage; the response is honest explanation + gauge evidence + sealing (chloride climate) + documentation. Panic and dismissal are both wrong.

choices.text: Tell them all concrete cracks and move on
choices.why: True and trust-destroying: 'it's normal' without the mechanism, the gauge, and the seal reads as brush-off — and this buyer talks to the next buyer.

choices.text: Promise slab replacement to protect the sale
choices.why: Replacing sound slabs over cosmetic shrinkage teaches the community that complaints mint concrete — and the replacement slab will shrink too.

choices.text: Refer them to the structural engineer for reassurance
choices.why: Escalating cosmetic hairlines to the EOR signals doubt where none exists and burns the engineer's time — reserve that phone call for the patterns that earn it.

quiz.explanation: PLAIN: know which cracks are normal, say why simply, prove it with a gauge, seal it because salt air. PRO: 'ID the pattern, document dormancy, seal per exposure, close on schedule.' The dual-register fluency is the customer-facing half of crack literacy. (V3-6)

quiz.teach: Corrosion cracks have a unique geometry: they follow the steel.
quiz.prompt: Year-2 balcony soffits show cracks running in straight lines with rust staining bleeding through. Why does this pattern jump the queue, and what's the investigation?

choices.text: Cracks ALONG bar lines + rust bleed = corrosion expanding inside the concrete — the long-fuse killer in this climate; scope a chain-drag/covermeter survey to map delamination and cover BEFORE pricing any repair, because the visible cracks are the mechanism's late stage
choices.why: Correct. Rust at 4–6x volume is jacking the cover off from within (S9); what you see is advanced. The survey defines the true extent — repairs priced off visible cracks alone always underscope.

choices.text: Shrinkage cracks that happened to align
choices.why: Shrinkage doesn't bleed rust or follow the reinforcement layout. Geometry along the bars IS the corrosion signature.
Tie stains are spots at tie locations. LINEAR staining along bar lines with cracking is expansion from inside — a different animal with a schedule.
Overload cracks run perpendicular to the main steel at the tension face (V3-1) — these run ALONG the bars. Reading the direction is the whole diagnostic.

quiz.explanation: PLAIN: straight rust-stained lines tracing the hidden steel mean the steel is rusting and swelling — and there's always more than shows. PRO: 'delamination along the bars — chain-drag the soffits, covermeter the cover, map before pricing.' Balconies + salt air + low cover is the V3-1/S3/S9 trifecta. (V3-6)

mathProblems.title: Surveying the soffits
mathProblems.context: Chain-drag/delamination survey priced per square foot across the suspect areas — the mapping that keeps corrosion repairs honestly scoped.

decisionPoints.title: The crack log
decisionPoints.scenario: Three years in, cracks of every family exist somewhere on the project: pour-day crazing on a pool deck, shrinkage lines in garage slabs, one monitored stair-step over a grouted void, sealed hairlines on the bulkhead cap. A new owner's-side building inspector (hired for an estate closing) photographs ALL of them into one alarming report titled 'Widespread Cracking Observed.' The buyer's attorney forwards it with a deadline.

options.label: Respond with your standing crack log: each photographed crack already identified by mechanism, gauged where warranted, sealed per exposure, with dates — plus an offer to walk the inspector through the diagnostic reasoning on site
options.outcome: The 'widespread cracking' report meets a document that classified every crack before the inspector found it. The attorney's deadline dissolves into a site walk where your super speaks both registers — and the closing proceeds on the strength of the paperwork you kept all along.

options.label: Have your engineer write a rebuttal calling the report alarmist
options.outcome: Dueling experts, no shared facts: without your own crack-by-crack record, the rebuttal is opinion against photographs — and photographs win deadlines. The engineer's letter costs more than the log would have and persuades less.

options.label: Send a crew to seal and paint every crack before responding
options.outcome: The inspector has photographs of cracks that are now mysteriously invisible — which reads exactly as it looks. Concealment after documentation is the one move that converts cosmetic cracking into a credibility problem with legs.

decisionPoints.debrief: Crack literacy pays twice: on site (right response, right speed) and on paper (the log that answers every future report). Identify by mechanism, gauge the questionable, seal per exposure, and WRITE IT DOWN — the diagnostic alphabet is also your legal defense. (V3-6, M10)
